tips.title: A million, not a hundred
tips.body: $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$, because the conversion is **cubed**. Dividing by 100 instead makes the answer ten thousand times too big — and no everyday solid is denser than about 20 000 kg/m³.

tips.title: Work in g and cm³, then times 1000
tips.body: $1$ g/cm³ is exactly $1000$ kg/m³. So divide grams by cm³ first — $108 \div 40 = 2.7$ — and multiply by 1000 at the end. Two conversions become one, and the risky one disappears.

tips.title: Compare with 1000 to decide floating
tips.body: Water is **1000 kg/m³**. Less than that floats, more sinks. And a steel ship floats because the **whole object** includes a great deal of **air**, so its *average* density is below water's — the steel's density has not changed.

tips.title: The spacing changes, never the particles
tips.body: Melting and boiling move particles **further apart**. They do not make them bigger, heavier or more numerous. Any answer that says the particles expand has lost the mark whatever else it gets right.

tips.title: Submerge it completely
tips.body: In the displacement method any part of the object above the water is volume you did not measure, so the density comes out too high. Push it under with a pin, and lower it on a thread so nothing splashes out.

steps.title: What density is
steps.body:
**Density** tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. It is what people mean when they say lead is *heavier* than wood — not that any piece of lead weighs more than any piece of wood, but that **the same volume** of it does.

$$\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \qquad \rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

- density, $\rho$ (the Greek letter *rho*), in **kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³**
- mass, $m$, in **kilograms, kg**
- volume, $V$, in **metres cubed, m³**

The units are worth pausing on, because they are where most marks are lost. A density in **kg/m³** needs the mass in **kilograms** and the volume in **metres cubed** — and a volume measured in cm³ is a very different number from one in m³.

$$1 \text{ m}^3 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$$

So the conversion between the two common density units is a factor of **1000**:

$$1 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$$

Water is **1000 kg/m³**, which is the same as **1 g/cm³** — a useful number to know, both as a check and because floating is decided by comparison with it.

steps.title: The particle model and the three states
steps.body:
The **particle model** pictures a material as particles — atoms or molecules — arranged differently in each state. It explains both **what the states are like** and **why their densities differ**, and the specification asks for both.

**Solid.** The particles are **packed closely together in a regular arrangement**, touching their neighbours. They vibrate about fixed positions but cannot move past one another. A solid keeps its **shape** and its **volume**.

**Liquid.** The particles are still **close together** but are **no longer in a fixed arrangement** — they can move past each other. A liquid keeps its **volume** but takes the **shape** of its container.

**Gas.** The particles are **far apart** and move **randomly at high speed**. A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume: it fills whatever it is in.

**Why the densities differ** follows directly. Density is mass per unit volume, and the particles themselves do not change — so what changes is how much **space** the same particles occupy:

- In a **solid** the particles are closest, so the most mass fits in a given volume: **highest density**.
- In a **liquid** they are slightly further apart, so the density is a little **lower**.
- In a **gas** they are very far apart, so a given volume contains very little mass: **by far the lowest density**.

That is the answer to *explain the difference in density between the states*: it is about the **spacing of the particles**, not their size or their mass.

steps.title: Changes of state
steps.body:
A **change of state** is when a substance moves between solid, liquid and gas. The specification names six:

- **melting** — solid to liquid
- **freezing** — liquid to solid
- **boiling** and **evaporating** — liquid to gas
- **condensing** — gas to liquid
- **sublimating** — solid straight to gas, with no liquid in between

Two facts about them are examinable, and both are easy to state badly.

**1. Mass is conserved.** When a substance changes state, **no particles are created or destroyed** — they are only rearranged. So the mass **before** the change equals the mass **after** it. Freeze 1 kg of water and you have 1 kg of ice. Boil it away and the steam still has the mass of the water it came from, even though it is nowhere near as dense.

**2. A change of state is a *physical* change, not a chemical one.** The difference the spec draws is precise:

**The material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.**

Melt ice and freeze it again and you have ice with exactly the properties you started with. Burn a piece of wood, and cooling the ash does not give you wood back — that is a **chemical** change, and it produces a **new substance**.

So the test for a physical change is **reversibility with the original properties restored**, not simply whether something looks different.

steps.title: Going deeper: the conversion that catches everyone
steps.body:
**Volume conversion is squared and cubed, and that is the whole difficulty.**

There are 100 cm in a metre. So there are:

- $100^2 = 10\,000$ cm² in a m²
- $100^3 = 1\,000\,000$ cm³ in a m³

Dividing a volume in cm³ by 100 instead of by a million gives an answer **ten thousand times too large**, and it is the single commonest error in density questions. A quick sanity check: no everyday solid has a density above about 20 000 kg/m³ (gold is 19 300), and none is below about 100. An answer of 2 700 000 has a conversion error in it.

**A shortcut worth knowing.** Because $1$ g/cm³ $= 1000$ kg/m³ exactly, you can work entirely in **g and cm³** and multiply by 1000 at the end. For the aluminium block: $108 \div 40 = 2.7$ g/cm³, then $\times 1000 = 2700$ kg/m³. That avoids two conversions and one of them is the risky one.

**Floating, explained properly.** An object floats if its density is **less than** that of the liquid. Wood (500 kg/m³) floats on water (1000 kg/m³); steel (7800) sinks. But a **steel ship floats**, and being able to explain that is a good discriminator: the ship is not solid steel — it contains a great deal of **air**, so the **average density of the whole ship** is less than water's. The material's density has not changed; the object's has.

**Mass is conserved, density is not.** When water freezes, the mass stays the same but the **volume increases** slightly, because water is unusual — its particles are held slightly further apart in ice. Since $\rho = m/V$ with $m$ fixed and $V$ larger, ice is **less dense** than water, which is why it floats on it. Most substances are denser as solids; water is the famous exception, and it is worth knowing as an exception rather than as the rule.

**Being exact about state changes.** Two phrasings lose marks:

- *The particles get bigger when something melts* — they do not. **The spacing between them changes**, never the particles themselves.
- *Mass increases when water boils because steam takes up more room* — volume and mass are different quantities. The **mass is unchanged**; the **density** falls.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Density** is mass per unit volume: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$, in **kg/m³**, with mass in **kg** and volume in **m³**.
- $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$, and $1 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
- **Water is 1000 kg/m³**, or 1 g/cm³.
- In a **solid** the particles are packed closely in a **regular arrangement**; in a **liquid** they are close but can move past each other; in a **gas** they are **far apart** and move randomly.
- Densities differ because of the **spacing** of the particles, not their size or mass: solid highest, gas by far the lowest.
- **Required practical 5**: a **regular** solid's volume comes from its **dimensions**; an **irregular** solid's from **displacement**; a liquid is weighed in a container and the container's mass subtracted.
- The object must be **fully submerged** for displacement to work.
- The six changes of state: **melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, sublimating**.
- **Mass is conserved** in a change of state — no particles are created or destroyed.
- A change of state is a **physical** change: the material **recovers its original properties if the change is reversed**.
- An object **floats** if its density is **less than the liquid's** — and a steel ship floats because the **whole object** includes air.
- The commonest error is dividing a volume in cm³ by 100 rather than by a **million**.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would determine the density of an irregularly shaped stone, naming the apparatus, and explain how you would reduce the main sources of error.
questions.solution: First the mass of the stone is measured using a balance, and recorded in kilograms. To find the volume, a measuring cylinder is partly filled with water and the level is read and recorded. The stone is then lowered gently into the water on a thread, and the new level is read. The stone displaces its own volume of water, so the volume of the stone is the difference between the two readings. This volume is in cubic centimetres and must be converted into cubic metres by dividing by one million. The density is then calculated by dividing the mass in kilograms by the volume in cubic metres. There are several sources of error. The stone must be completely submerged, because if any part of it is above the water the volume measured will be too small; a thin pin can be used to push it under. It should be lowered gently on a thread so that no water splashes out of the cylinder, which would make the volume reading wrong. The water level should be read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus, to avoid a parallax error.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Measuring the mass.** Use a **balance**, and record the mass in **kilograms**.

**Measuring the volume by displacement.**

1. Part-fill a **measuring cylinder** with water and read the level.
2. **Lower the stone gently** into the water on a thread.
3. Read the new level.
4. The stone **displaces its own volume**, so the volume is the **difference** between the readings.

**Calculating.** Convert the volume from cm³ to m³ by dividing by **1 000 000**, then

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

**Reducing the errors.**

- The stone must be **completely submerged** — any part above the water makes the volume too small. Push it under with a thin pin.
- **Lower it gently on a thread** so no water splashes out.
- Read the level at **eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus**, to avoid a parallax error.

The volume is where nearly all the error in this practical sits, which is why all three precautions are about measuring it rather than the mass.

questions.prompt: Use the particle model to explain the differences in density between the solid, liquid and gas states of the same substance, and explain what happens to the mass of a substance when it changes state.
questions.solution: In the solid state the particles are packed closely together in a regular arrangement, touching one another, so a given volume contains a large number of particles and therefore a large mass. This gives the solid the highest density. In the liquid state the particles are still close together but are no longer in a fixed arrangement and can move past one another, so they are on average slightly further apart. A given volume therefore contains slightly less mass, and the density is a little lower than that of the solid. In the gas state the particles are very far apart and move randomly at high speed, so a given volume contains very few particles and very little mass, which makes the density of a gas far lower than that of either the solid or the liquid. It is important to note that the particles themselves are identical in all three states; what changes is the spacing between them. When a substance changes state the mass is conserved, because no particles are created or destroyed and the same particles are simply rearranged, so the mass before the change is equal to the mass afterwards even though the volume, and therefore the density, may change a great deal.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Solid.** The particles are **packed closely in a regular arrangement**, touching. A given volume holds many particles and so a large mass: the **highest density**.

**Liquid.** The particles are still **close together** but no longer in a fixed arrangement, so on average slightly **further apart**. A given volume holds slightly less mass: a **little lower** density.

**Gas.** The particles are **far apart**, moving randomly at high speed. A given volume holds very few particles and very little mass: **by far the lowest** density.

**The key point.** The particles are **identical** in all three states. What changes is the **spacing between them** — never their size or their mass. An answer saying the particles get bigger or heavier has the physics wrong.

**Mass in a change of state.** It is **conserved**. No particles are created or destroyed; the same particles are simply rearranged. So the mass before equals the mass after — even though the **volume**, and therefore the **density**, may change a great deal.

examTechnique.body:
Convert the units before substituting, and say which conversion you are doing. A volume in cm³ divides by a million to become m³.

For a regular solid find the volume from the dimensions; for an irregular one use displacement and say the object must be fully submerged.

When explaining a difference in density, talk about the spacing of the particles, not their size.

For a floating question, compare the object's density with the liquid's, and for a hollow object say that the average density of the whole object is what matters.

In a change of state question, say that mass is conserved because no particles are created or destroyed.

Sanity check the answer: everyday solids run from a few hundred to about 20 000 kg/m³.
examinerErrors: Dividing a volume in cm³ by 100 rather than by 1 000 000.
Leaving the mass in grams while giving the density in kg/m³.
Saying the particles get bigger when a substance melts.
Saying mass increases when a liquid boils because the gas takes up more space.
Forgetting to subtract the container's mass when finding the density of a liquid.
Not fully submerging the object in the displacement method.
Saying a steel ship floats because steel floats when it is shaped into a hull.
Giving a density with no unit.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer converts units before it substitutes and writes the conversion down, so a marker can see where the factor of a million went. It explains density differences by the **spacing** of particles and says explicitly that the particles themselves are unchanged. Asked about a floating ship, it distinguishes the density of the **material** from the density of the **object**, and its explanation predicts what happens when the hull is holed. It knows mass is conserved in a change of state and can give the reason rather than the fact. And it sanity checks the final number against the range real materials occupy.
